title: ITA Section 37(1.1): SR&ED Pool Adjustments Legislation
description: Learn about ITA Section 37(1.1) legislation in Canada and how SR&ED pool adjustments work for R&D expenditures across related Canadian corporations.
summary: This page explains SR&ED pool adjustments under section 37 of Canada's federal Income Tax Act for businesses claiming SR&ED. Government and non-government assistance reduces the Section 37 pool in the year expenditures are incurred, federal ITCs applied or refunded reduce it the following year, and any negative balance is included in taxable income under paragraph 12(1)(t).

body.text: This page explains SR&ED pool adjustments under section 37 of Canada's federal Income Tax Act for businesses claiming SR&ED. Government and non-government assistance reduces the Section 37 pool in the year expenditures are incurred, federal ITCs applied or refunded reduce it the following year, and any negative balance is included in taxable income under paragraph 12(1)(t).
Executive Overview of the Canadian R&D Tax Architecture

Canada maintains one of the most mature and financially substantial research and development (R&D) tax incentive regimes among Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) jurisdictions. Anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program, the Canadian system distributes more than $4 billion in federal tax assistance annually across upwards of 20,000 corporate and unincorporated claimants. Unlike discretionary grant mechanisms that depend on competitive budgetary allocations, the federal SR&ED program operates as an entitlement-based statutory tax incentive embedded directly within the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) and administered jointly by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) and the Department of Finance Canada. While the Department of Finance Canada establishes the legislative policy framework under the Income Tax Act, the CRA is responsible for operational administration, technical and financial claim verification, and the issuance of binding administrative guidelines. When layered with provincial and territorial R&D tax credits, direct non-repayable innovation contributions such as the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), and specialized clean technology investment tax credits, the Canadian fiscal framework can offset between 40% and 75% of eligible R&D labour and capital outlays depending on corporate structure and provincial nexus.

The Canadian SR&ED landscape underwent its most consequential legislative transformation in over a decade through measures first announced in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement, formally introduced in Budget 2025, and enacted into law via Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Applicable retroactively to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024—and to depreciable property acquired or equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024—Bill C-15 fundamentally recalibrated the economics of Canadian R&D investment. Specifically, the legislation doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3 million to $6 million, widened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out corridor from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended eligibility for the 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and fully restored the eligibility of capital expenditures and shared-use equipment (SUE) after an eleven-year statutory hiatus. Concurrently, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched a formal voluntary pre-claim approval process utilizing Form T1322, enabling businesses to secure multi-year technical eligibility determinations prior to filing their annual corporate income tax returns.

body.text: Statutory Foundation and the Dual-Pool Mechanics of the Income Tax Act

The Canadian federal SR&ED regime is governed by three interlocking provisions of the Income Tax Act operating in tandem with Part XXIX (Section 2900) of the Income Tax Regulations. First, subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act establishes the authoritative legal definition of "scientific research and experimental development" across all federal and harmonized provincial tax statutes. Second, Section 37 of the Income Tax Act governs the accumulation and deduction of the cumulative pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures carried out in Canada, as well as permissible foreign support work under subsection 37(1.5). Third, Sections 127 and 127.1 of the Income Tax Act govern the quantification of "qualified expenditures" for Investment Tax Credit (ITC) purposes, the application of the 15% basic and 35% enhanced ITC rates, the associated corporation expenditure limit rules, and the cash refundability mechanics under subsection 127.1(1).
Section 37 Deduction Pool versus Section 127 Qualified Expenditure Pool

A foundational principle of Canadian R&D tax auditing is that computing an SR&ED claim requires two related yet legally distinct statutory calculations that deliver two separate fiscal benefits. The first calculation determines the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures under Section 37, which is reported in Part 3 of Form T661, whereas the second calculation determines the pool of qualified SR&ED expenditures for the Investment Tax Credit under Section 127, which is reported in Part 4 of Form T661. Tax practitioners and corporate controllers must never treat "allowable SR&ED expenditure" and "qualified SR&ED expenditure" as interchangeable terms, because an expenditure may be fully deductible under Section 37 without generating an equivalent dollar base for the Section 127 ITC, and conversely, certain notional or shared-use amounts may generate Section 127 ITCs without entering the Section 37 deduction pool.

Under subsection 37(1), a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may deduct current SR&ED expenditures—and, for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, qualifying capital SR&ED expenditures—incurred in the taxation year, or elect to leave all or a portion of those expenditures in an undeducted Section 37 pool that carries forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in future taxation years. This indefinite carryforward mechanism is strategically vital for pre-profit biotechnology, clean technology, and advanced manufacturing enterprises whose R&D deductions would otherwise expire after 20 taxation years if claimed immediately and converted into ordinary non-capital losses under paragraph 111(1)(a).

The Section 127 qualified expenditure pool diverges structurally from the Section 37 deduction pool across four critical statutory dimensions. First, when a claimant elects to use the Proxy Method to compute overhead, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—calculated at 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base on Line 820 of Form T661—is a purely notional amount added exclusively to the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool to generate ITCs. The PPA is never added to the Section 37 deduction pool; instead, actual overhead expenses such as utilities, shop supplies, and administrative support remain deductible as ordinary business expenses under Section 9 of the Income Tax Act. Second, while 100% of an eligible arm's-length SR&ED contract payment made to a Canadian subcontractor is deductible in the Section 37 pool, subsection 127(9) restricts the Section 127 qualified expenditure inclusion to 80% of the contract expenditure (and 80% of eligible third-party payments), thereby eliminating the subcontractor's estimated commercial profit margin from the federal tax credit base. Third, under the restored capital expenditure rules effective after December 15, 2024, depreciable equipment used primarily (more than 50% but less than 90% of its operating time) in SR&ED does not enter the Section 37 deduction pool and must instead be depreciated under standard Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) classes on Schedule T2SCH8. Nevertheless, such Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) generates Section 127 ITCs on Line 504 of Form T661 in two equal instalments: 25% of the capital cost in the first period (first-term SUE) and 25% in the second period (second-term SUE). Fourth, under subsection 127(26)—which applies for the purposes of the investment tax credit definitions in subsection 127(9)—and subsection 78(4), salaries, wages, or other SR&ED amounts accrued at year-end but remaining unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year are excluded from both the Section 37 deduction pool and the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool for that year, only becoming eligible in the subsequent taxation year in which they are actually paid.
Recapture, Super-Deduction Mechanics, and Paragraph 12(1)(t) Income Inclusion

To prevent taxpayers from claiming both a 100% tax deduction and a tax-free investment tax credit on the exact same dollar of expenditure, the Income Tax Act enforces a rigorous statutory assistance and recapture mechanism. Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(9), any government assistance or non-government assistance that a taxpayer receives, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of SR&ED reduces both the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool in the taxation year in which the expenditure is incurred.

Provincial and territorial R&D tax credits—such as the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit, the Québec tax credit for research, innovation and commercialization (CRIC), or the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant—are legally classified as government assistance in the taxation year in which the underlying SR&ED expenditures are incurred. Consequently, provincial R&D credits directly reduce the federal Section 127 qualified expenditure pool in the current taxation year before the federal 15% or 35% ITC is computed. By contrast, the federal SR&ED ITC itself does not reduce the current year's Section 127 pool; instead, any federal SR&ED ITC that is either applied to reduce Part I tax payable or refunded in cash in a given taxation year reduces the Section 37 deductible SR&ED pool in the following taxation year. Where the deduction of a prior-year federal ITC drives the Section 37 pool balance below zero, the negative balance is included directly in the taxpayer's taxable business income in that following taxation year pursuant to paragraph 12(1)(t) of the Income Tax Act. Similarly, if a claimant subsequently repays government assistance or a contract payment that previously reduced its qualified expenditure pool, the repayment generates an ITC determined at the rate that would have been earned in the year the assistance or contract payment was originally received.

Furthermore, with the restoration of SR&ED capital expenditures after December 15, 2024, the SR&ED ITC recapture rules under subsections 127(27) to 127(35) once again carry vital audit significance. If a claimant acquires depreciable property after December 15, 2024, claims an SR&ED ITC on that property (either as 90%+ All or Substantially All capital on Line 390 or as SUE on Line 504), and subsequently sells the property or converts it to commercial (non-SR&ED) use within 20 taxation years, the claimant must add back ("recapture") the lesser of the ITC originally earned on the property and the applicable ITC percentage multiplied by the proceeds of disposition (or fair market value at the time of conversion) directly to its federal Part I tax—and provincial corporate tax in jurisdictions such as Ontario and Alberta—otherwise payable for the taxation year of disposition or conversion.
Landmark Legislative Modernization: Bill C-15 and the 2024–2026 SR&ED Reforms

The enactment of Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, represents the most expansive enhancement to the federal SR&ED program since the mid-1990s. Designed to stem the outflow of Canadian intellectual property and encourage scale-up enterprises and capital-intensive manufacturers to anchor R&D operations domestically, the Bill C-15 amendments apply to taxation years that begin after December 15, 2024, as well as to depreciable property acquired or equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024.
Expansion of the Enhanced 35% Expenditure Limit and the Subsection 127(10.2) Taper Formula

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 doubled the baseline annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% federal ITC from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000. Consequently, a qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC)—or an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC)—can now earn up to $2,100,000 in 100% refundable federal SR&ED tax credits annually ($6,000,000 multiplied by 35%), doubling the previous statutory ceiling of $1,050,000. Qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in excess of the corporation's available expenditure limit continue to earn the basic 15% federal ITC rate, of which 40% is refundable in cash for a qualifying CCPC, yielding an effective 6% cash refund alongside a 9% non-refundable tax credit that can be carried back 3 taxation years and carried forward 20 taxation years.

Concurrently, Bill C-15 widened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds governing the expenditure limit for CCPCs. Under the amended subsection 127(10.2) of the Income Tax Act, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit remains completely unreduced until the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the claimant and all associated corporations exceeds $15,000,000 (increased from the legacy $10,000,000 threshold), and tapers linearly to zero at $75,000,000 (increased from the legacy $50,000,000 ceiling).
The statutory taper formula in subsection 127(10.2) of the Income Tax Act is expressed mathematically as:
Expenditure Limit = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000

Within this statutory formula, variable A is nil ($0) whenever the aggregate taxable capital employed in Canada for the immediately preceding taxation year across the claimant and all associated corporations is $15,000,000 or less. Where prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000, variable A is defined as the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000. Expressed in marginal terms, every $10.00 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada above the $15,000,000 threshold reduces the $6,000,000 expenditure limit by $1.00. Crucially, prior-year taxable income does not enter the federal formula under subsection 127(10.2); following the repeal of the federal taxable income phase-out in 2019, a highly profitable taxation year does not by itself shrink a CCPC's federal SR&ED expenditure limit. Furthermore, under the Bill C-15 amendments, CCPCs may alternatively elect to have their $6,000,000 expenditure limit phased out using the gross-revenue-based phase-out structure established for Eligible Canadian Public Corporations rather than the taxable capital formula.

body.text: Specific anti-avoidance and proration rules apply under subsection 127(10.5) and related provisions of the Income Tax Act when allocating the $6,000,000 expenditure limit among associated CCPCs or consolidated ECPC groups. If a CCPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year and is associated in two or more of those taxation years with another CCPC that has a taxation year ending in that same calendar year, the corporation's allocated expenditure limit for a short taxation year is prorated based on the ratio of the number of days in the short taxation year to 365. For example, if two associated corporations allocate a $6,000,000 expenditure limit equally ($3,000,000 to each corporation) and one corporation has a short taxation year running 184 days from July 1 to December 31, its expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.5) is prorated to $1,512,329 ($3,000,000 multiplied by 184 divided by 365). Moreover, under subsection 256(2.1), two or more corporations are deemed to be associated with each other if one of the main reasons for the separate existence of those corporations in a taxation year is to reduce the amount of income tax otherwise payable or to increase the amount of refundable SR&ED ITCs available.
Extension of Enhanced Refundability to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)

Historically, a Canadian technology or life sciences company that completed an Initial Public Offering (IPO) or reverse takeover on the Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX) or TSX Venture Exchange immediately lost its CCPC status under subsection 125(7), causing its federal SR&ED rate to drop from a 35% cash-refundable credit to a 15% strictly non-refundable credit. To eliminate this structural penalty against domestic public capital formation, Bill C-15 amended Section 127 of the Income Tax Act to grant Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) access to the enhanced 35% refundable ITC on up to $6,000,000 of qualified SR&ED expenditures for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024.

To qualify as an ECPC throughout a taxation year, a corporation must be resident in Canada, have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange in Canada (or have elected to be a public corporation), and must not be controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatever by one or more non-resident persons. Because public corporations frequently do not compute Part I.3 taxable capital on the same basis as private corporations, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit for an ECPC phases out based on the corporation's—and its consolidated corporate group's—average prior-year gross revenue rather than taxable capital, tapering linearly between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 of average annual gross revenue. Just as associated CCPCs must share the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, an ECPC that has more than one taxation year ending in a calendar year and is a member of a consolidated group in which another ECPC has a taxation year ending in that same calendar year must allocate the $6,000,000 limit across the consolidated group.
Restoration of Capital Expenditures and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) Post-December 15, 2024

Between January 1, 2014 and December 15, 2024, capital expenditures on depreciable property and lease payments for capital-type equipment were completely excluded from the federal SR&ED program. Bill C-15 reversed that decade-long exclusion by restoring SR&ED eligibility for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, applicable to both the Section 37 deduction pool and the Section 127 ITC pool.

The restored capital expenditure regime operates across three distinct statutory tracks depending on whether the asset is purchased for dedicated SR&ED use, purchased for shared commercial and SR&ED use, or leased. Under the first track, covering All or Substantially All (ASA) depreciable capital property reported on Line 390 of Form T661, an expenditure made to acquire new or used depreciable property after December 15, 2024 qualifies in full as an SR&ED capital expenditure if, at the time the property becomes available for use, the claimant intended either to use all or substantially all (defined administratively as 90% or more) of the operating time of the property in its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada, or to consume all or substantially all (90% or more) of the value of the property to perform SR&ED in Canada. Land is statutorily excluded because it is a non-depreciable asset, and buildings (or leasehold interests in buildings) remain excluded under paragraph 37(8)(e). Depreciable property claimed as an SR&ED capital expenditure on Line 390 of Form T661 is 100% deductible in the Section 37 pool and earns full Section 127 ITCs at the 35% or 15% rate; consequently, property claimed on Line 390 must never be included on Schedule T2SCH8 for Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) purposes. Furthermore, claimants reporting capital expenditures on Line 390 must complete Lines 262 and 263 in Part 2 of Form T661, listing the names of the 10 most expensive SR&ED depreciable properties acquired after December 15, 2024 and used in each claimed project.

Under the second track, covering Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) reported on Line 504 of Form T661, new depreciable equipment (excluding general-purpose office equipment or furniture) acquired after December 15, 2024 that does not meet the 90% ASA threshold but is used primarily (more than 50% of its operating time) for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada qualifies for partial ITC inclusion. The capital cost of SUE is not added to the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures; instead, the claimant must depreciate the equipment under regular Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) rates and rules on Schedule T2SCH8. For Section 127 ITC purposes—calculated identically under both the Traditional Method and the Proxy Method—the claimant claims on Line 504 of Form T661 25% of the capital cost of the equipment that was used primarily in SR&ED in the first period (first-term SUE) and the other 25% of the capital cost in the second period (second-term SUE). Thus, up to 50% of the capital cost of shared-use machinery and laboratory equipment earns the 35% or 15% federal ITC across two taxation years.

Under the third track, governing leased equipment costs, any lease costs incurred before December 16, 2024 remain ineligible for SR&ED tax incentives. For lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, where leased equipment is used ASA (90% or more) of its operating time in SR&ED, the lease payments qualify under both the Traditional and Proxy methods, except that claimants using the Proxy Method cannot include lease costs for general-purpose office equipment or furniture (GPOEF) because such costs are covered by the 55% PPA. Conversely, when a claimant elects the Traditional Method, the claimant may claim the SR&ED-attributable portion of lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 for equipment used in SR&ED less than 90% of the time on Line 360 of Form T661 as overhead and other expenditures. Generally, operating time means the time the equipment usually runs or functions. If a claimant's taxation year began before December 16, 2024 and straddles that effective date, the claimant must calculate SR&ED use as a percentage of total operating time occurring strictly after December 15, 2024. Similarly, on Lines 535 and 540 of Form T661—which govern non-arm's-length capital transfers and contract capital deductions—claimants may only include amounts related to depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024.
Launch of the Voluntary Pre-Claim Approval Process (Form T1322)

Effective April 1, 2026, the CRA launched a formal, voluntary Pre-Claim Approval Process designed to provide upfront technical eligibility certainty to R&D performers before they file their annual income tax returns. Accessed electronically through the CRA's My Business Account portal by submitting Form T1322, the mechanism allows corporations to submit proposed or ongoing R&D projects for upfront technical evaluation by CRA Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs).

Once approved by the CRA, a pre-claim project determination can remain valid for a period of up to three consecutive taxation years, subject to the conditions of the program and provided the technical scope of the project remains consistent with the approved application. Crucially, pre-claim approval via Form T1322 does not replace Form T661 or the annual expenditure claim. While pre-claim approval establishes the eligibility of the proposed scientific or technological work under subsection 248(1), the claimant must still file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 annually with its corporate income tax return by the statutory 18-month reporting deadline to substantiate that the work was performed and to establish the final quantum of allowable and qualified expenditures.
Scientific and Technological Eligibility: Subsection 248(1) and Jurisprudence

The substantive gateway to all federal and provincial R&D tax incentives in Canada is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, which generally conforms to the OECD Frascati Manual. Under subsection 248(1), SR&ED is defined as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis".
Categories of Qualifying Work and the Eight Exhaustive Support Work Categories

Subsection 248(1) divides eligible scientific and technological activities into three core research categories—set out in paragraphs (a), (b), and (c)—and one derivative category of directly supporting activities under paragraph (d). Paragraph 248(1)(a) encompasses basic research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Basic research is typically carried out in a laboratory setting, frequently involves third-party payments to universities, research institutes, or consortia, and yields results published in scientific journals. A classic example of basic research cited in CRA administrative policy is theoretical and experimental physics investigating elementary particles—such as devising experiments to demonstrate the physical existence of the electron and measure its mass and charge—at a stage where no practical device or commercial application was envisioned.

Paragraph 248(1)(b) encompasses applied research, which is likewise work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge, but conducted with a specific practical application in view. For instance, private-sector investigations into the physical properties of semiconductors and how electrons behave within them—undertaken with the specific commercial objective of discovering the principle of controlled conductivity to eventually build a solid-state semiconductor amplifier before any physical device or prototype had been constructed—constitute applied research.

Paragraph 248(1)(c) encompasses experimental development, defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements. Accounting for the vast majority of private-sector SR&ED claims in Canada, experimental development translates scientific principles into functional technological capabilities. Following the discovery of the principle of the transistor through applied research, the subsequent engineering and testing of working prototypes and fabrication techniques to manufacture solid-state amplifiers and transistors exemplifies experimental development. Developing a working transistor after discovering its underlying scientific principle did not advance pure scientific knowledge, but it achieved a technological advancement—defined as an advancement in the practical application of scientific knowledge and principles.

Paragraph 248(1)(d) governs support work, which is strictly restricted to eight exhaustive statutory categories: engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, and psychological research. Support work under paragraph 248(1)(d) is never SR&ED on its own. To qualify as part of an SR&ED claim, work falling within one of those eight enumerated categories must satisfy a dual nexus test: its scope must be commensurate with the needs of, and directly in support of, basic research, applied research, or experimental development work that is undertaken in Canada.
Statutory Exclusions Under Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k) and the Purpose Test

Immediately following the inclusionary categories, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) of the Income Tax Act establish seven absolute statutory exclusions from the definition of SR&ED. Specifically, the statute excludes market research or sales promotion under paragraph (e); quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes under paragraph (f); research in the social sciences or the humanities under paragraph (g); prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas under paragraph (h); the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process under paragraph (i); style changes under paragraph (j); and routine data collection under paragraph (k). Collectively referred to as the statutory exclusions, this work cannot be claimed, though CRA guidelines specify that excluded work should only be delineated and carved out after the claimant has identified that core eligible SR&ED work has been performed. For example, a mining enterprise may conduct eligible experimental development on a novel metallurgical extraction process while simultaneously prospecting for minerals; the company may file an SR&ED claim for its eligible experimental development, but all work relating to mineral prospecting must be excluded under paragraph 248(1)(h).

In CRA technical reviews, the boundary between eligible support work under paragraph 248(1)(d)—such as data collection or testing—and excluded work under paragraphs 248(1)(f) and (k)—such as routine testing or routine data collection—is governed by the Purpose Test. Auditors evaluate why the activity was performed: if data collection or testing is carried out specifically for the purpose of performing basic research, applied research, or experimental development by testing a hypothesis, it qualifies as eligible support work under paragraph 248(1)(d). Conversely, if the identical physical testing or data gathering is performed for commercial quality assurance, regulatory compliance sign-off, or routine operational monitoring, it is statutorily excluded.
Judicial Precedents and the CRA's Consolidated "Why" and "How" Framework

The legal interpretation of subsection 248(1) has been forged by a foundational body of Tax Court of Canada and Federal Court of Appeal jurisprudence, anchored by the landmark decision of Justice Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC), and consistently affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Canada, 99 DTC 5087 (FCA), CW Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, and Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 FCA 355. In Northwest Hydraulic, the Tax Court of Canada established the five-question jurisprudential test for determining whether a project constitutes SR&ED. First, the Court asks whether there was a scientific or technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or habitual, standard practice. Second, the Court asks whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that scientific or technological uncertainty. Third, the Court examines whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. Fourth, the Court evaluates whether the process resulted in a scientific or technological advancement. Fifth, the Court requires verification that a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results was kept as the work progressed.

In its current administrative doctrine—the Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives, which replaced the legacy 2012/2015 Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy—the CRA consolidated the five Northwest Hydraulic questions into a unified Two-Requirement Framework ("The Why" and "The How") derived directly from the unchanged statutory text of subsection 248(1).

cells: Work must be conducted to advance scientific knowledge or achieve a technological advancement by overcoming an underlying scientific or technological uncertainty.

Technological uncertainty exists when publicly available scientific/engineering knowledge and standard practice within the claimant's business environment are insufficient. Indicators include: existing design methods are inapplicable; specifications conflict with established standards; excessive interdependent variables exist; operating parameters fall outside normal ranges; or incompatible technologies must be integrated. Acquiring off-the-shelf or third-party proprietary know-how via training or hiring consultants does not qualify.
Work must be a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis performed by qualified personnel.

Must follow the four-step scientific method: (1) defining the problem and formulating a hypothesis consistent with known facts; (2) testing the hypothesis through controlled experiment or mathematical/engineering analysis (allowing the hypothesis to evolve iteratively); (3) developing logical conclusions based on measurable, countable results; and (4) retaining contemporaneous documentation (notebooks, commits, test logs, dated emails, failure analyses) generated as the work progressed.

body.text: A critical legal principle affirmed both by Northwest Hydraulic and CRA policy is that SR&ED is a knowledge-generation program, not a commercial new-product success program. If a systematic experimental investigation fails to achieve the desired commercial product performance—yet generates logical conclusions explaining why a given technological hypothesis or architecture cannot function under specific boundary conditions—that advancement in technological knowledge fully satisfies the "technological advancement" criterion. Conversely, if a company's research efforts merely uncover an existing off-the-shelf solution that resolves the challenge, or if a study's end results cannot be measured or counted, the work will not qualify as SR&ED.
Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures (QREs) and Calculation Methodologies

Once a project's technical activities are validated under subsection 248(1), the claimant must quantify its allowable SR&ED expenditures in Part 3 of Form T661 and its qualified SR&ED expenditures in Part 4 of Form T661 in accordance with Section 37, Section 127, and Income Tax Regulation 2900.
Traditional Method versus Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Election

At the time of filing Form T661 for a taxation year, a claimant must elect on Line 160 in Part 3, Section A to compute its SR&ED claim using either the Proxy Method or the Traditional Method. This election applies across all SR&ED projects for that taxation year and cannot be changed once Form T661 has been filed for that year.

Under the Proxy Method, which is elected by the vast majority of Canadian SR&ED claimants, the taxpayer does not specifically track or claim overhead expenditures on Form T661. Instead, the claimant calculates a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) on Line 820 in Part 5, Section B of Form T661 equal to 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base reported on Line 818, subject to the statutory salary-base restrictions and the overall PPA cap. For every $100,000 of eligible directly engaged SR&ED salary base, the 55% PPA adds $55,000 of notional overhead to the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool, bringing the ITC-bearing expenditure base to $155,000. As explained above, the PPA is a notional amount used strictly to calculate qualified expenditures for the Section 127 ITC and is never added to the Section 37 deduction pool, while actual overhead expenditures remain deductible as ordinary business expenses under Section 9 of the Income Tax Act.

Conversely, under the Traditional Method, the claimant enters "0" for the PPA and instead specifically identifies, tracks, and substantiates actual overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661 throughout the taxation year. To qualify on Line 360, an overhead expenditure must be directly attributable or directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada—including, for expenses incurred after December 15, 2024, the SR&ED-attributable portion of lease costs for equipment used in SR&ED less than 90% of the time. The Traditional Method is generally advantageous only for facility-intensive industrial operations where directly incremental facility overhead and non-ASA equipment leases exceed 55% of directly engaged technical payroll.
Directly Engaged Labour, Specified Employee Caps, and the 10% Foreign Work Rule

Salaries and wages represent the foundational cost component of Canadian SR&ED claims and simultaneously govern the magnitude of the 55% PPA calculation. To be claimable, salaries and wages must be paid to employees who are "directly engaged" in the prosecution of SR&ED. Under CRA administrative policy and Regulation 2900, "directly engaged" refers strictly to hands-on technical work, such as performing experiments, writing experimental source code, engineering prototypes, analyzing test data, or providing direct first-line technical supervision of experimental activities. Whether an employee is directly engaged in SR&ED is determined solely by the tasks that are performed and never by the employee's corporate job title. Clerical, administrative, human resources, legal, accounting, and executive management activities are excluded from directly engaged salaries because they are accounted for through the 55% PPA or Traditional overhead.

While all SR&ED work must generally be performed inside Canada, subsection 37(1.5) of the Income Tax Act—reported on Lines 307 and 309 of Form T661—permits a claimant to include salaries and wages for SR&ED work performed outside Canada after February 25, 2008, up to a strict statutory ceiling of 10% of the total eligible SR&ED salaries and wages for work performed in Canada during the taxation year. Three rigid statutory conditions govern this foreign salary allowance. First, the SR&ED activities performed outside Canada must be performed directly by employees of the claimant who are residents of Canada under the Income Tax Act (meaning mere Canadian citizenship or presence on a Canadian payroll is insufficient if residency is lost, and foreign subcontractors never qualify regardless of percentage). Second, the foreign work must be directly undertaken by the claimant, related to its business, and solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada by the claimant, rather than independent foreign R&D. Third, the 10% ceiling is calculated on the aggregate Canadian SR&ED salary pool rather than on a per-employee basis, meaning a single Canadian-resident employee may work entirely abroad on specialized testing if their salary remains under 10% of total Canadian SR&ED wages, and these eligible foreign wages on Line 309 also qualify for the 55% PPA salary base in Part 5 of Form T661.

Additional statutory restrictions apply to "specified employees," defined in subsection 248(1) as employees who either own, directly or indirectly, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation (or a related corporation) or do not deal at arm's length with the corporation. Because owner-managers exercise control over their own compensation structures, the Income Tax Act prohibits claiming bonuses, profit-based remuneration, or taxable stock option benefits paid to specified employees, and caps a specified employee's total allowable Part 3 SR&ED salary at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under the Canada Pension Plan (CPP), prorated by the number of days employed in the taxation year. Furthermore, for purposes of calculating the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) salary base in Part 5 of Form T661 (leading to Line 818), each specified employee's includable salary is restricted to the lesser of 75% of the employee's total salary and wages and 2.5 times the YMPE, prorated for the number of days employed in the year. Under official CRA payroll declarations, the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) is $68,500 for 2024, $71,300 for 2025, $74,600 for 2026, and $76,700 for 2027 (announced by the CRA on October 28, 2026). Consequently, for a full 365-day 2026 calendar taxation year, a specified employee's maximum direct Part 3 SR&ED salary (5 times YMPE) is $373,000, and their maximum Part 5 PPA salary base inclusion (2.5 times YMPE) is $186,500.
Materials Consumed or Transformed, Arm's-Length Contracts, and Third-Party Payments

Beyond direct technical payroll and the 55% PPA, three major expenditure categories populate the Section 37 and Section 127 pools. On Line 320 and Line 325 of Form T661, claimants may include the cost of physical materials that are either consumed (destroyed or rendered virtually valueless) or transformed (physically integrated into an experimental prototype, pilot plant, or trial batch) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. If transformed materials embedded in an experimental prototype or custom unit are subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, the SR&ED recapture rules apply to claw back the ITC earned on the material component.

On Line 370 of Part 3 of Form T661, payments to arm's-length Canadian subcontractors who perform basic research, applied research, experimental development, or paragraph 248(1)(d) support work in Canada on behalf of the claimant are 100% deductible in the Section 37 pool, but are restricted under subsection 127(9) to an 80% inclusion in the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool. Consequently, for a qualifying CCPC or ECPC at the 35% enhanced rate, arm's-length Canadian subcontractor expenditures generate an effective federal tax credit of 28% (80% multiplied by 35%), while corporations at the 15% basic rate earn an effective federal credit of 12% (80% multiplied by 15%). Similarly, third-party payments made to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or non-profit SR&ED research consortia are subject to the 80% Section 127 inclusion rule, provided the SR&ED is carried out in Canada, is related to the claimant's business, and the claimant is entitled to exploit the results. Agricultural producers making contributions to approved agricultural organizations for SR&ED are not required to complete Form T661 for those contributions and instead report them directly on Schedule 31 (T2SCH31), Part 8, Line 350. While physical consumables and eligible capital equipment qualify, the acquisition of off-the-shelf software, licences, and intellectual property rights is non-eligible under the federal SR&ED program.

body.text: Cross-Border Structuring, Corporate Control, and Transfer Pricing Governance

Foreign multinational enterprises and cross-border venture-backed technology companies operating in Canada must structure their corporate ownership, intercompany R&D agreements, and intellectual property (IP) arrangements with precision to avoid forfeiting enhanced tax credit rates or triggering transfer pricing reassessments. Following the enactment of Bill C-15, foreign investors and multinational groups navigate three distinct structural routes in Canada.
De Jure and De Facto Control Under Subsection 256(5.1)

Under the first route, where a foreign parent corporation establishes a wholly-owned Canadian subsidiary to conduct R&D in Canada, the subsidiary is controlled by a non-resident corporation and therefore does not qualify as a CCPC under subsection 125(7). Founders and non-specialist advisors frequently miscalculate budgets by assuming that any newly incorporated Canadian subsidiary earns the 35% enhanced rate, whereas a wholly-owned subsidiary of a US, UK, or other foreign parent is restricted to the 15% basic non-refundable federal ITC, which can be carried back 3 years and carried forward 20 years against Canadian Part I corporate income tax. When combined with provincial credits and the 55% PPA, public or foreign-owned corporations (or CCPCs exceeding the phase-out limit) can still achieve combined federal-provincial tax credits of up to approximately 36% of eligible salaries, up to 18% of eligible subcontractor fees, and up to 24% of materials consumed or transformed.

Under the second route, where foreign venture capital funds or strategic corporate investors acquire a minority equity stake in a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC) while Canadian residents retain control, the entity preserves its CCPC status and earns the 35% fully refundable federal ITC on up to $6,000,000 of qualified expenditures, plus 15% (40% refundable) above that threshold. However, Canadian tax law tests both de jure (legal voting) control and de facto (factual) control under subsection 256(5.1) of the Income Tax Act. If a foreign minority investor holds board control, unilateral decision veto rights, or financing rights that effectively direct the corporation, the CRA can take the position that CCPC status is lost, stripping away the 35% refundable rate retroactively.

Under the third route, newly created by Bill C-15 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)—including Canadian-listed public subsidiaries with foreign-listed parents where control is not held by non-residents—can access the 35% enhanced refundable federal ITC on up to $6,000,000 of qualified SR&ED expenditures, subject to the gross-revenue phase-out.

body.text: Post-November 2025 Transfer Pricing Overhaul and Intellectual Property Ownership

In cross-border corporate structures—particularly where a foreign minority investor or foreign parent is simultaneously a customer, supplier, or intellectual property licensor to the Canadian R&D performer—intercompany pricing arrangements and IP ownership clauses face heightened audit scrutiny. Under Bill C-15, Parliament overhauled Canada's transfer pricing rules in Section 247 of the Income Tax Act, effective for taxation years beginning after November 4, 2025. The modernized transfer pricing regime requires that cross-border R&D cost-sharing, contract R&D reimbursements, and IP licensing arrangements be defensible on economic substance grounds rather than mere paper contracts. As industry audit experience demonstrates, deficient transfer pricing documentation and misaligned IP ownership are among the most common ways the net financial benefit of a cross-border SR&ED structure is eroded during a CRA audit.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Every Canadian province (except Prince Edward Island) and the Yukon Territory supplements the federal SR&ED program with a dedicated provincial or territorial R&D tax credit. Except for Québec (administered independently by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (administered by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration), all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits piggyback directly on the federal subsection 248(1) definition of SR&ED and are administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) through provincial schedules filed with the T2 Corporation Income Tax Return.

Because provincial and territorial R&D tax credits constitute government assistance under subsection 127(9) of the federal Income Tax Act, they reduce the federal Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool in the taxation year in which the expenditures are incurred. Consequently, the combined federal-provincial effective credit rate is calculated sequentially: the provincial credit is computed first, and the federal 35% or 15% ITC is then applied to the net qualified expenditure pool remaining after subtracting the provincial credit.
Ontario: OITC (Schedule 566), ORDTC (Schedule 508), and OBRITC (Schedule 568)

Ontario operates a three-tier suite of corporate R&D tax credits administered by the CRA under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), which can be claimed concurrently on eligible SR&ED expenditures performed in Ontario by a corporation with a permanent establishment in Ontario.

The primary incentive for small and medium-sized corporations is the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), claimed on Schedule 566 (T2SCH566). For taxation years commencing after May 31, 2016, the OITC provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit (reduced from 10% for taxation years ending before June 1, 2016) on up to $3,000,000 of qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario, yielding a maximum annual cash refund of $240,000. Unlike the federal expenditure limit, which doubled to $6,000,000 under Bill C-15, Ontario's OITC annual expenditure limit remains capped at $3,000,000 and must be shared among associated corporations and prorated for short taxation years. Crucially, the $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit is subject to a dual phase-out mechanism: it is gradually reduced if the associated group's prior-year federal taxable income exceeds $500,000 (and is completely eliminated at $800,000), or if the prior year's taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $25,000,000 (and is completely eliminated at $50,000,000). Ontario has harmonized its OITC qualified expenditure rules with the federal Bill C-15 capital restoration: qualified Ontario expenditures include 100% of current expenditures and 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024 (whereas capital expenditures made after December 31, 2013 and before December 16, 2024 were excluded, and capital expenditures made before January 1, 2014 were included at 40%).

The second Ontario incentive is the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), claimed on Schedule 508 (T2SCH508). For taxation years commencing after May 31, 2016, the ORDTC provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (reduced from 4.5% prior to June 1, 2016) on all eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures net of the OITC and OBRITC, with no annual expenditure cap. Available to all corporations—both CCPCs and large or foreign-controlled enterprises—the non-refundable ORDTC offsets Ontario corporate income tax (which is levied at an 11.5% general rate and a 3.2% small business rate on the first $500,000 of active business income for CCPCs with taxable capital below $15 million) and can be carried back 3 years and carried forward 20 years. Because both the OITC and the ORDTC constitute government assistance that reduces the federal Section 127 qualified expenditure pool, Ontario law allows a corporation to formally waive all or part of its ORDTC or OITC by providing a written waiver with its T2 return filed within 6 months after the end of the taxation year (or on an amended return for that year), enabling non-taxable CCPCs to avoid reducing their 35% federal cash refund.

The third Ontario incentive is the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC), claimed on Schedule 568 (T2SCH568), which provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario under an eligible contract with an approved Ontario research institute, subject to a $20,000,000 annual expenditure cap shared across an associated group of corporations.
Québec: Revenu Québec Administration, the CRIC and the Legacy Form RD-1029.7 Series

Québec operates an autonomous provincial R&D tax credit system administered by Revenu Québec alongside the provincial CO-17 corporate income tax return. For taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec replaced its legacy R&D tax credits with a single refundable credit, the tax credit for research, innovation and commercialization (CRIC), which Revenu Québec also calls the tax credit for R&D, innovation and pre-commercialization. The CRIC replaces the tax credit for salaries and wages (R&D), the tax credit for university research or research carried out by a public research centre or a research consortium, the tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium, the tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research, the tax credit for technological adaptation services, the industrial design component of the design tax credits, and the tax holiday for foreign researchers and experts. The CRIC is fully refundable at a basic rate of 20%, increased to 30% on up to $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures that exceed the applicable exclusion threshold, regardless of the value of the corporation's assets; the exclusion threshold is the greater of $50,000 and the sum of the R&D employees threshold and the pre-commercialization employees threshold. Qualified expenditures include salaries and wages, consideration paid to subcontractors, payments to certain research organizations, and capital expenditures to acquire property used for R&D or pre-commercialization activities carried out in Québec, and the CRIC is claimed on Form RD-1029.8.CR filed with the corporate income tax return.

For taxation years beginning before March 26, 2025, corporations conducting SR&ED in Québec claim provincial incentives through four specialized Revenu Québec forms. First, under Form RD-1029.7 (Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D), accompanied by Form RD-1029.7.8 for agreements allocating the $3,000,000 expenditure limit among associated corporations), Québec provides a fully refundable tax credit on eligible R&D salaries and wages and 50% of eligible Québec R&D subcontractor fees. While the historical credit rates prior to June 5, 2014 ranged from 17.5% to 37.5%, the post-2014 regime provides a basic refundable rate of 14% and an enhanced refundable rate of up to 30% for Canadian-controlled corporations on up to $3,000,000 of eligible expenditures, subject to a sliding-scale exclusion threshold based on corporate asset size. Second, under Form RD-1029.8.6 (Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium), corporations claim a refundable credit of 14% to 30% (historically 35% prior to June 5, 2014) on 80% of eligible research contract payments. Third, under Form RD-1029.8.9.03 (Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium), members of an eligible research consortium claim a 14% to 30% refundable credit (historically 35%) on their pro-rata share of consortium R&D expenses. Fourth, under Form RD-1029.8.16.1 (Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research), corporations claim a 14% to 30% refundable credit (historically 35%) on qualifying collaborative pre-competitive R&D expenditures.
Alberta: Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) and Incremental Base-Level Mechanics

Following the expiration of the legacy 10% Alberta SR&ED tax credit on December 31, 2019, the Government of Alberta introduced the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) effective January 1, 2021 under Sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act. Administered by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) under the policy leadership of the Ministry of Technology and Innovation and detailed in Information Circular IEG-1, the IEG is delivered directly through the Alberta corporate tax system as a refundable tax credit.

The IEG provides qualified corporations that undertake R&D in Alberta after December 31, 2020 with a two-tier refundable payment on up to $4,000,000 in annual eligible R&D spending—matching federal qualified SR&ED expenditures, including the Alberta proxy amount and restored capital expenditures—for a maximum annual funding payout of $800,000. Specifically, the corporation receives an 8% base payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's base level of spending, and an enhanced 20% payment (representing the 8% base payment plus an additional 12% incremental payment) on eligible Alberta R&D spending that exceeds the corporation's base spending level. A firm's base level of spending is calculated as the corporation's average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the immediately preceding two taxation years. Consequently, a first-time Alberta claimant—or a growing company that incurred zero Alberta R&D spending in the prior two taxation years—has a base spending level of zero and receives the full 20% refundable credit on 100% of its eligible Alberta R&D expenditures up to $4,000,000.

To focus support on small and medium-sized businesses, the IEG phases out incrementally for corporations whose prior-year taxable capital exceeds $10,000,000 and is completely eliminated for firms with $50,000,000 or more in taxable capital. Partnerships, trusts, and individuals are not eligible for the IEG. Eligible corporations claim the grant when filing their Alberta Corporate Income Tax Return (AT1) by submitting AT1 Schedule 29 (Form AT29 / Form A29), alongside supporting project schedule Form AT4970 (Listing of Innovation Employment Grant Projects Carried Out in Alberta) and legacy schedule AT238 (AT1 Schedule 16) where applicable. While the statutory filing deadline for the IEG is 15 months after the corporation's AT1 filing due date (i.e., 21 months after year-end), TRA will not process or disburse IEG payments until the qualifying expenditures have been verified by the CRA under the federal SR&ED program. Because the federal SR&ED claim must be submitted within 18 months of the fiscal year-end, Alberta claimants must in practice file their federal and provincial claims within the 18-month federal window.
British Columbia, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Atlantic Canada, and Yukon

Across the remaining Canadian provinces and territories, R&D tax credits provide vital regional incentives, with Manitoba, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Yukon offering refundable credits to both SMEs and large or foreign-controlled corporations. In Manitoba, under Section 7.3 of the Income Tax Act (Manitoba) and claimed on Schedule 380 (T2SCH380), corporations earn a 15% tax credit on eligible expenditures made after April 11, 2017 (reduced from 20% prior to that date). Where the R&D is carried out under contract with a qualifying post-secondary or research institution, the entire 15% Manitoba credit is fully refundable; for in-house R&D, one-half of the credit (7.5%) is refundable in cash for all corporations (regardless of size or foreign ownership) and the remaining 7.5% is non-refundable with a 3-year carryback and 20-year carryforward. As a result, a large or foreign-controlled corporation in Manitoba earns a 30% combined gross R&D credit (15% federal + 15% Manitoba, including 7.5% in cash), nearly double the 18.5% combined non-refundable rate (15% federal + 3.5% ORDTC) available to an equivalent large company in Ontario. Furthermore, a corporation may renounce all or part of its Manitoba R&D tax credit up to 1 year after its T2 filing due date, though for federal tax purposes any renunciation must be executed on or before 6 months after the corporation's taxation year-end.

body.text: Comprehensive Quantitative Modelling of Federal and Provincial Claim Stacking

To demonstrate the exact statutory interaction between the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA), provincial government assistance reductions, and federal Section 127 ITC calculations under the post-December 15, 2024 Bill C-15 rules, consider a qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC) with prior-year taxable capital under $10,000,000 and prior-year federal taxable income under $500,000. Assume the corporation incurs $1,000,000 in directly engaged Canadian R&D salaries paid to regular (non-specified) employees and $200,000 in eligible ASA (90%+) R&D depreciable equipment acquired after December 15, 2024.

Under the Proxy Method, the claimant's gross Section 127 qualified expenditure pool before government assistance equals $1,750,000—comprising $1,000,000 of direct salaries, $550,000 of notional PPA overhead ($1,000,000 multiplied by 55%), and $200,000 of restored ASA capital equipment. Concurrently, its Section 37 deductible expenditure pool before government assistance equals $1,200,000 ($1,000,000 salaries plus $200,000 capital equipment, because the $550,000 notional PPA never enters Section 37).

When an Ontario CCPC is in a tax-loss position and cannot immediately utilize the non-refundable 3.5% ORDTC ($56,350), claiming the ORDTC reduces its net federal qualified expenditure pool by $56,350, which in turn reduces its immediate 35% federal cash refund by $19,722 ($56,350 multiplied by 35%), lowering immediate cash received from $703,500 to $683,778. By filing a written waiver of the ORDTC within 6 months of its taxation year-end, the pre-profit Ontario CCPC preserves its federal qualified expenditure pool and maximizes its immediate cash refund at $703,500.
Complementary Direct Funding, Clean Economy ITCs, and Government Assistance Stacking

A core structural advantage of the Canadian innovation ecosystem is the ability to stack non-repayable direct government grants and clean technology investment tax credits alongside federal and provincial SR&ED claims. However, claimants must rigorously model the interaction between direct grants and tax credits, because failure to disclose every government funding source on Form T661 constitutes a primary compliance violation on audit.
NRC IRAP and the Prescribed Proxy Amount Stacking Leverage Effect

The National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) is Canada's premier direct R&D contribution program for small and medium-sized enterprises. Alongside core firm R&D contributions—which have supported approximately 5,500 projects since 2010 with a median award of $22,548 (and a middle-half distribution ranging from $9,000 to $59,000)—NRC IRAP operates specialized streams including Youth Employment, Green Youth, AI Assist, Clean Technology, and the IP Assist Program (which has funded approximately 340 intellectual property strategy contributions since 2021 with a median award of $16,030). In standard R&D project agreements, NRC IRAP reimburses up to 80% of eligible internal technical R&D labour costs.

While an NRC IRAP reimbursement constitutes government assistance that reduces the qualified SR&ED expenditure pool so that a claimant can only claim SR&ED on the remaining unreimbursed expenditure it paid itself, the statutory mechanics of the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) create a major stacking advantage. Under Part 5 of Form T661, the 55% PPA on Line 820 is calculated on the gross eligible SR&ED salary base on Line 818 before the NRC IRAP grant is deducted as government assistance in Part 4. Consequently, if a qualifying CCPC incurs $100,000 in eligible R&D salary and receives an $80,000 (80%) NRC IRAP grant, the corporation still generates $55,000 in notional PPA overhead on the full $100,000 salary, bringing gross qualified expenditures to $155,000. Subtracting the $80,000 IRAP grant leaves $75,000 in net qualified SR&ED expenditures ($20,000 unreimbursed salary plus $55,000 PPA), which earns $30,150 in combined Ontario OITC (8%, with ORDTC waived) and federal SR&ED (35%) cash refunds—yielding $110,150 in total non-dilutive cash funding on a $100,000 direct salary outlay.
Clean Economy Investment Tax Credits and Regional Development Agency Contributions

Beyond NRC IRAP, Canadian R&D performers can integrate specialized federal and provincial capital, digital media, and commercialization incentives into their funding stack. At the federal level, the Clean Economy Investment Tax Credits—comprising the Clean Technology ITC, Clean Hydrogen ITC, Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage (CCUS) ITC, and the Clean Technology Manufacturing ITC—operate as entitlement-based capital tax credits with no competitive application review. The Clean Technology ITC provides up to a 30% refundable credit (reduced to 20% without prevailing wage and apprenticeship labour compliance) on solar, wind, geothermal, heat pumps, energy storage, and small modular nuclear equipment, while the Clean Technology Manufacturing ITC provides up to a 30% refundable credit on clean technology manufacturing machinery. Because government assistance reduces the capital cost base used to calculate an ITC and double-dipping on the same asset is prohibited, claimants must segregate experimental pilot assets claimed under the restored SR&ED capital rules from commercial clean technology assets claimed under the Clean Economy ITCs.

At the regional and provincial level, key complementary programs include the Ontario Made Manufacturing Investment Tax Credit, which provides a 15% tax credit on up to $20,000,000 per year of eligible manufacturing or processing buildings, machinery and equipment that become available for use on or after May 15, 2025 (up to $3,000,000 annually, refundable for CCPCs and non-refundable for non-CCPCs, repayable if the asset leaves Ontario within five years, for expenditures incurred through December 31, 2029). Software and digital entertainment firms in Ontario also utilize the Ontario Interactive Digital Media Tax Credit (OIDMTC), which provides a 40% refundable credit on eligible Ontario labour (and up to $100,000 of marketing and distribution costs per product) for non-specified products and a 35% credit for fee-for-service work, provided an Ontario Creates certificate is applied for within 18 months of year-end. Additional commercialization and R&D instruments include FedDev Ontario's Business Scale-up and Productivity (BSP) program (median contribution of $1.8 million, with the middle half of awards between $1.0 million and $2.8 million), CanExport Innovation (direct R&D export grants for international R&D partnerships), the Northern Ontario Heritage Fund Corporation (NOHFC) INVEST North Innovation Stream (grants up to $2,000,000), Alberta Innovates Vouchers (up to $100,000), and the Alberta Carbon Capture Incentive Program (a 12% grant on eligible CCUS capital costs).
Compliance Governance, Form T661 Architecture, Filing Deadlines, and CRA Audit Defence

Because an SR&ED claim is a statutory self-assessed filing integrated into the taxpayer's annual income tax return rather than a standalone grant application, strict compliance with prescribed forms, line-item disclosures, and statutory filing deadlines is mandatory.
Line-by-Line Structural Breakdown of Form T661 and Part 9 Preparer Penalties

To access the Section 37 deduction and the Section 127 ITC, a claimant must complete and submit Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim)—prepared in accordance with CRA Guide T4088—together with Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) for corporations or Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals)) for unincorporated individuals.

Section B: Allowable current and capital expenditures (Lines 300–305 domestic wages; Lines 307–309 foreign SR&ED wages ≤10% cap; Line 320/325 materials consumed/transformed; Line 360 Traditional overhead and <90% post-Dec 15, 2024 equipment leases; Line 370 contracts; Line 390 restored ASA 90%+ capital expenditures acquired after Dec 15, 2024). body.text: A strict statutory penalty enforces Part 9 (Claim Preparer Information) of Form T661: if complete and accurate claim preparer information is missing or omitted from Part 9, a $1,000 penalty applies under the Income Tax Act, for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally liable. Furthermore, the CRA explicitly cautions claimants that when signing the SR&ED tax credit application, the taxpayer bears full legal responsibility for ensuring that the claim is compliant, even if the claimant was misled by third-party promotional representations.
The 18-Month Statutory Filing Bar and CRA Review Protocols

Under subsections 37(11) and 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, an SR&ED claim is governed by a rigid statutory filing deadline of 18 months after the end of the corporation's taxation year (12 months after the corporation's 6-month T2 filing due date). Failure to file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 containing the prescribed project-by-project technical narratives and project cost allocations on or before the 18-month reporting deadline results in the permanent statutory disallowance of the expenditures and ITCs for that taxation year.

Once submitted, SR&ED claims are processed under established CRA service standards, with approximately 90% of claims accepted as filed in FY2024–25. If a CCPC files its return within 6 months of its fiscal year-end, the CRA typically processes the refundable claim within 4 months (120 days, or up to 180 days if selected for review), whereas non-CCPC claims can take up to 12 months to process. Because waiting up to 18 months from the start of a fiscal year to receive an SR&ED cash refund can create working-capital constraints, many technology companies utilize private SR&ED financing to obtain cash advances on accrued SR&ED credits as early as 3 months into their taxation year.

When a claim is selected for verification by the CRA, it is routed through one of four review pathways: a Desktop Review, a Financial Review (conducted in accordance with the SR&ED Program Financial Claim Review Manual to verify T4s, invoices, proof of payment, and assistance deductions), a combined Technical and Financial Review, or a First-Time Claimant Advisory Services (FTCAS) educational meeting. During a Technical and Financial Review, CRA Research and Technology Advisors evaluate the Part 2 narratives (Lines 242, 244, and 246) and inspect contemporaneous documentation—such as dated lab notebooks, project diaries, source-code logs, emails, meeting minutes, and employee time-tracking records—that was recorded at the time the work was completed.
Strategic Conclusions and Tax Governance Recommendations

The enactment of Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1) on March 26, 2026 has fundamentally elevated the financial return of conducting R&D in Canada. To capture the full benefit of the modernized statutory framework while insulating claims from CRA technical or financial disallowance, corporate tax directors, chief financial officers, and R&D leaders should institutionalize five core governance practices.

First, organizations that ceased tracking laboratory, manufacturing, and pilot-plant capital assets after the 2014 repeal must immediately reconfigure fixed-asset accounting and engineering logbooks for depreciable property acquired and equipment leases incurred after December 15, 2024. Technical teams must maintain operating-time records to substantiate either the 90%+ All or Substantially All (ASA) threshold—claimed on Line 390 of Form T661, itemized on Lines 262–263, and excluded from Schedule T2SCH8 CCA—or the >50% Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) threshold, which is depreciated on Schedule T2SCH8 while generating 25% first-term and 25% second-term ITCs on Line 504.

Second, mid-market CCPCs with prior-year taxable capital between $10 million and $75 million—as well as Canadian-listed public corporations qualifying as Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)—should remodel their multi-year R&D capital allocations for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 to capture up to $2,100,000 in 35% refundable federal ITCs under the expanded $6,000,000 expenditure limit. Concurrently, CCPCs with high balance-sheet taxable capital but moderate gross revenue should evaluate electing into the gross-revenue phase-out structure introduced under Bill C-15.

Third, following the April 1, 2026 launch of the CRA's voluntary Pre-Claim Approval process, corporations embarking on multi-year, capital-intensive R&D initiatives should submit Form T1322 via My Business Account to secure up to three years of upfront technical eligibility certainty, while maintaining rigorous annual expenditure tracking for their mandatory Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 filings.

Fourth, claimants operating across provincial jurisdictions should optimize their government assistance stacking and waiver elections. Specifically, pre-profit Ontario CCPCs should model the cash-flow impact of the non-refundable 3.5% ORDTC (Schedule 508) and execute a written waiver within 6 months of year-end whenever preserving the 35% federal refundable pool maximizes immediate liquidity. Simultaneously, SMEs across Canada should pair NRC IRAP salary grants with the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) to generate SR&ED tax credits on their unreduced gross technical salary base.

Fifth, technical and legal teams must embed contemporaneous hypothesis-driven documentation directly into their engineering workflows—recording technological uncertainties, explicit hypotheses, test results, and time tracking as the work progresses rather than reconstructing narratives at year-end. Finally, cross-border enterprises must audit shareholder agreements to protect de facto CCPC control under subsection 256(5.1), monitor Canadian-resident employee foreign travel to remain within the 10% aggregate salary cap on Lines 307 and 309, and align intercompany R&D agreements with Canada's post-November 4, 2025 transfer pricing substance rules under Bill C-15.
